desc:
rows is a list of integer lists that may have different lengths (each has at least one element). Every individual list is sorted in non-decreasing order, but nothing is promised between different lists. Values may repeat.

Imagine all values from all lists poured into one sorted sequence (duplicates count separately). Return the k-th smallest value, where k = 1 is the smallest.
constraints: 1 ≤ rows[i].length ≤ 200 and the total number of values is at most 6,000
Each rows[i] is in non-decreasing order
hints: Sorting everything works in O(N log N) for N values, but the sorted rows are not being used.
Think about the reverse question: for a number x, how many values are ≤ x? In a sorted row that is one binary search.
The k-th smallest is the smallest x in [min of row starts, max of row ends] whose count of values ≤ x is at least k. Binary search on x, and count with bisect_right in every row.
editorial: Let count(x) be the number of values ≤ x over all lists; it is non-decreasing in x. The k-th smallest value is the smallest x with count(x) ≥ k: at that x the count first reaches k, which can only happen at a value that actually occurs, and duplicates are handled because they all raise the count together.

Computing count(x) takes one bisect_right per list, O(R log L) for R lists of length up to L. The value range is about 2 * 109, so the outer binary search needs about 31 iterations: O(R log L log V) in total, with O(1) extra space.
A k-way merge with a heap also works, at O(k log R). The value-space search is preferable when k is large, and it is the same idea as the 'median of a row-sorted matrix' problem.
